# Cannon and artillery (`cannon_artillery`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs gunpowder; helped by copper_bronze, blast_furnace_cast_iron, boring_machine, lost_wax_casting, ballistics_gunnery
- Core idea: A strong tube closed at one end, a powder charge, a wad and a ball that fits the bore closely, fired through a small touch hole. Early bombards were built like barrels from wrought-iron staves and hoops and threw huge stone balls a few times a day. The decisive design, complete in France and Burgundy by the 1490s, is a long bronze gun cast in one piece like a bell, firing cast-iron balls (three times as dense as stone, so a smaller, thicker-walled gun hits harder), with trunnions cast on its sides so that it pivots for elevation on a two-wheeled carriage drawn by horses. Such guns keep up with an army and open a medieval curtain wall in hours instead of weeks.
- Pitfalls:
  - Reloading without swabbing out smouldering remains with a wet sponge and stopping the vent; the new charge fires in the loader's face
  - Cast-iron guns burst without warning, bronze guns bulge first; early cast iron needs far thicker walls
  - A ball that fits loosely wastes the gas and bounces down the bore; a ball that jams bursts the gun
  - Forgetting the carriage, the draught animals and the powder supply, which are most of the system
  - Claiming cannon ended fortification; within fifty years the bastioned trace restored the advantage of the defence
- History: china: late 13th c. – Heilongjiang gun associated by context with events of 1287–88; the Xanadu gun bears a date equivalent to 1298; 14th c. – cast-iron cannon; europe: 1326 – first picture (Walter de Milemete) and first record (Florence orders cannon and iron balls); 15th c. – great bombards; 1450s–1470s – trunnions and wheeled carriages; 1494 – Charles VIII's train of about 40 mobile bronze siege guns in Italy; in 1490 Italian states still use slow stone-throwing bombards hauled by oxen; islamic: 1360s – Mamluk cannon securely attested (claims for 1260 are disputed); 1453 – Ottoman bombards breach the walls of Constantinople; 1683 – the Ottoman army before Vienna brings mostly light and medium guns and has to rely on mining; east_asia: 1370s – Korean cannon against pirates; 1592 – Korean naval guns defeat Japanese fleets; india: 15th c. – guns in the Deccan and Gujarat; 1526 – Babur's field guns at Panipat
- Read:
  - Bert S. Hall, Weapons and Warfare in Renaissance Europe (1997)
  - Carlo M. Cipolla, Guns and Sails in the Early Phase of European Expansion, 1400–1700 (1965)
  - Tonio Andrade, The Gunpowder Age (2016)
